paraphrase: Maitreya approached Parāśara, the best of sages who knows the three times, bowed with folded hands and asked: 'Lord, jyotiṣa is the supreme, holy and secret Vedāṅga, with three branches — horā, gaṇita and saṃhitā; of these three the horā is said to be the best; I wish to hear it from you.'

paraphrase: The supreme Self shines in all beings, and all this rests in the supreme Self. In all beings there are two portions, the portion of the individual soul (jīvāṃśa) and the portion of the supreme Self (paramātmāṃśa). The Sun and the other planets, and Brahmā, Kāma, Dveṣa and others, have the supreme Self's portion predominant, as do the powers Śrī and the rest; in others the jīva-portion predominates.

paraphrase: Having bowed to Brahman, to its power Bhāratī, and to the Sun, lord of planets and cause of the world's origin, Parāśara will tell the eye of the Veda (vedanayana) as he heard it from the mouth of Brahmā.

paraphrase: This should be given to one who is calm, devoted to the teacher, always truthful and a believer (āstika); then he will attain the good. It must not be given to another's pupil, to an unbeliever or to a deceitful person: if given, sorrow arises day by day, without doubt.

paraphrase: Viṣṇu is one, unmanifest, beginningless, the Lord, pure sattva, without qualities yet endowed with the three; with one portion he creates and protects the whole world in play, while three quarters of him are immortal. As Vāsudeva he is both manifest and unmanifest; with his powers Śrī (sattva), Bhū (rajas) and Nīlā (tamas) he takes the forms Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna and Aniruddha; from them come mahat, ahaṃkāra and Brahmā; the threefold ahaṃkāra yields the gods, the senses and the elements. With Śrī Viṣṇu protects, with Bhū Brahmā creates, with Nīlā Śiva devours.
notes: Pāñcarātra-style vyūha cosmogony. Phase-B spot check: wording/locator matched against a local e-text in sources_raw/ (GRETIL / eBhāratī / bilara-data); not a formal Phase-C sourcing check.

paraphrase: Thus all has been told in which everything comes to be; those who know it know what has been and what will be. Without jyotiṣa no one can ever know this; therefore it must be studied, by brahmins especially. The man who condemns jyotiṣa without knowing the śāstra suffers the Raurava hell and blindness in another birth.

paraphrase: To destroy the strength of the daityas, increase the strength of the gods and establish dharma, the auspicious avatāras were born from the planets in order: Rāma from the Sun, Kṛṣṇa from the Moon, Narasiṃha from Mars, the Buddha from Mercury, Vāmana from Jupiter, Paraśurāma (Bhārgava) from Venus, the Tortoise from Saturn, the Boar from Rāhu and the Fish from Ketu; other (incarnations) too are born of the planets.

paraphrase: Those in whom the supreme Self's portion is greater are called sky-goers (divine); those in whom the jīva-portion is greater are called jīvas. From the planets come forth the portions of the supreme Self as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa and the other avatāras, who merge back into them when their work is done; from their jīva-portions men and others are born, who also merge there and into the unmanifest.

paraphrase: The significators beginning with the Self (ātmakāraka) are seven, from the Sun to Saturn, or eight including Rāhu (used when two planets have equal degrees; some always count eight). The ātmakāraka is the planet with the most degrees in its sign (then minutes, then seconds); the one with the least is the last kāraka; Rāhu's degrees are counted backward from thirty.

paraphrase: Counting from Kṛttikā, three times over, the lords of the periods are the Sun, Moon, Mars, Rāhu, Jupiter, Saturn, Mercury, Ketu and Venus; the remainder of the count from Kṛttikā to the birth-asterism divided by nine gives the first lord. A full life is 120 years, so in the Kali age the Viṃśottarī is the chief period-system. The years are, in order: 6, 10, 7, 18, 16, 19, 17, 7 and 20.

paraphrase: There are many kinds of periods (daśā): chief is the Viṃśottarī; some hold the Aṣṭottarī, some the Ṣoḍaśottarī, Dvādaśottarī, Pañcottarī, Śatābdikā, Caturaśītisamā, Dvisaptatisamā, Ṣaṣṭisamā and Ṣaṭtriṃśatsamā — these depend on the asterisms; also the Kāla, Cakra and Kālacakra periods, the Cara, Sthira, Kendra, Kāraka, Brahmagraha, Māṇḍūka, Śūla, Yogārdha, Dṛg, Trikoṇa, Rāśi, Pañcasvara and Yoginī periods, the Paiṇḍī, Āṃśī and Naisargikī, the Aṣṭavarga, Sandhyā and Pācaka periods, and others such as the Tārā; not all are accepted by all.

paraphrase: The yoga by which people leave home for another religious order: when four or more strong planets are in one sign, renunciation arises according to the strongest — from the Sun a tapasvin, from the Moon a kāpālika, from Mars one wearing red cloth, from Mercury an ekadaṇḍin, from Jupiter a yati, from Venus a cakradhara, from Saturn a nirgrantha. If those planets are set in the Sun's rays, even though strong, the persons are not initiated but devoted to that order.

paraphrase: Maitreya asks: the śāstras say there is no good destination for the sonless — by what sin is one sonless, how can astrologers know it from the ascendant, and what is the remedy? paraphrase: The planets' images are to be made of copper, crystal, red sandalwood, gold (two), silver, iron, lead and bronze, or painted on cloth in their colours in their directions: the Sun two-armed on a lotus seat with lotuses in a seven-horsed chariot; the Moon white, in white, with a club, on a ten-horsed chariot; Mars four-armed, red, with spear, trident and club, on a ram; Mercury yellow, on a lion, with sword, shield and club; Jupiter and Venus yellow and white, four-armed, with staff, rosary and water-pot; Saturn dark blue, on a vulture, with trident, bow and arrow; Rāhu on a lion, fierce-faced, blue; the Ketus smoke-coloured on vultures — all crowned and granting boons.
